section.name: The (a,b,c) scenario worked through
section.t: In the agentproto mailing-list discussion of July 2026, in the thread on the draft minutes of the AGENTPROTO BoF, Stephen Farrell posed a gating scenario . In his words:

li.t: If (a,b,c) is a comms path between agents (perhaps within a tree) and if 'c' is actually a newly created entity, but one that needs access to a long-term secret credential accessible at 'a' (e.g. pwd or SSH private key) and where that credential must not be exposed to 'b' nor easily abused - then how's that going to work?

section.t: He emphasized that "the scenario I posited is one where 'b' creates 'c' and so is in a fine place to cheat" .
The list discussion produced concrete mitigations, collected in a reply by Shawn Sammartano , who credited most of them to existing mechanisms:

li.t: exact, single-use, attenuated permission slips bound to request bytes;
hardware-protected keys, and threshold signing;
short-lived credentials, and forward-moving counters;
delegation budgets, and delays with cancellation windows;
approval separated from the creator. Sammartano also stated the hard case plainly: "If b builds c, then b can read c's key, so b can be c. No message format fixes that, mine included."

section.t: The author proposed an enforcement/observation framing in response to that discussion . The control-topology test of refines that framing by distinguishing adversary-resistant detection coverage from a particular finding made from evidence already obtained. Farrell posed the scenario. This document does not attribute the generalized test to him. Applied to the scenario:

li.t: Exact, single-use, attenuated authority bounds what the grant authorizes, where it is enforced. It does not establish that an action attributed to c was not performed by b, where b created or hosts c and can obtain or invoke c's signing capability (rules 2 and 6 of ).

A prevention claim at that boundary needs an enforcement point b does not control and cannot circumvent. A claim that covered misbehavior cannot be concealed needs evidence b cannot forge, on a path b cannot silently prune (). Attestation and threshold signing supply such points only in deployments that actually place them outside b's control.
What is missing in the hard case is not another field. It is a point outside b's control that either enforces or observes, and no message format creates one.

section.t: This is narrower than solving credential custody. It makes the assurance claim and its trust boundary reviewable before a mechanism is chosen, which is what a chartering or design review needs.

section.name: Three public findings
section.t: Three public findings state the same bounds outside agent systems, in the words of the bodies that made them.

In the English prosecutions arising from the Post Office Horizon accounting system, the Court of Appeal found that the prosecutor "treated what was no more than a shortfall shown by an unreliable accounting system as an incontrovertible loss", and that defendants were convicted "on the basis that the Horizon data must be correct, and cash must therefore be missing, when in fact there could be no confidence as to that foundation" . The load-bearing premise was the reliability of that system. The court recorded that the prosecutor was under a duty to investigate subpostmasters' claims that there were problems with it, and it found "failures of investigation and disclosure". On the reading taken here, that is the position rule 9 of names. The claim rested on a premise the relying party was required to test and did not adequately test. The judgment does not address what a bounded report of the same evidence would have said, and it is not cited for that part of the rule.

In the inquiry into the Grenfell Tower fire, the panel examined the performance criteria applied in large-scale fire tests of external wall systems. Failure to meet those criteria would show a system unlikely to comply with the applicable requirement. But "the converse was not necessarily true": a system might meet the criteria and yet fail to comply with that requirement . A bounded test result can tell against a claim in one direction without establishing it in the other.

In the third case the test results were genuine outputs of a genuine test. Vehicles were certified against emissions standards on the strength of those results . Software detected the test condition and enabled full emissions controls only then, so the vehicles "meet emissions standards in the laboratory or testing station, but during normal operation" emitted nitrogen oxides at levels up to forty times the standard . The result established the behavior of the vehicle under the conditions the test applied, which was all it had ever observed. The certificate carried it to a claim about the vehicle in use (rule 11 of ).
These authorities reached findings within their own legal and regulatory settings. The findings are their own, and their connection to the rules stated here is this document's reading.

section.name: Changes
section.t: This appendix is to be removed before publication as an RFC.

li.t: adds a Certificate Transparency example that distinguishes a signed incorporation promise, evidence of inclusion, consistency of the checked log states, detection coverage, and a particular detection. The example states its client-policy and control assumptions.

distinguishes an accurate authorization-status report from the grounds that the reported result was available to or used by the decision-maker considering whether an activity may continue. It makes the reference time for current status part of the appraisal context, covers consultations that return no current answer, and leaves admission policy separate.

is added alongside the existing reference. The Acknowledgments credit Blake Morrison's contributed CT example. The development disclosure distinguishes work on -01 from the additions in this revision.

The evidence-law example makes the conditions and limits of self-authentication explicit. The InterPARES reference identifies its editor, the Rule 902 reference distinguishes amendment and compilation dates, and the Bu and Abak references cite updated revisions. Small wording changes clarify terminology and non-inference rules 2 and 12; CT and CA are expanded at first use.
No protocol, record format, registry, result-code set, or new numbered non-inference rule is introduced.

Independence is defined once, as limits on three capabilities of a named party or coalition: forgery, concealment, and circumvention (Sections and ). The earlier definition treated them as one property. no longer repeats the audit example, which stays in .
adds a note on the RATS terms.

says in which sense this document uses "support", adds a practical test of it, and points to the routes of . Its first bound and the abstract now name what evidence constitutes or proves, not only what it observed.

no longer describes the bases as ordered. They are distinct questions about one action. It now points to for claims about an effect, and it separates the observation base from an observation in the sense used elsewhere in the document.
speaks of kinds of claim rather than claim dimensions.

adds rules 11 to 13: behavior observed under different conditions, multiplicity of sources, and the coherence of an account produced by the interested party. Rules 1 to 10 keep their numbers. Rule 2 adds attribution along a delivery path. Rule 3 no longer reads matching records as agreement between the parties. Rule 4 limits itself to the authenticity of individual records, and rule 7 to the boundary's own observation. The last sentence of rule 9 now follows the reporting terms of . The preamble is shorter.

revises four items: item 3 names the three capabilities, item 5 no longer says that a signature or registration supplies no evidence, item 7 asks which route of , or which other stated basis, supports a claimed effect, and item 10 follows .

adds a route through evidence whose verification establishes a predicate. It adds a qualification on the time and finality of an observed effect, and it names as an idealization the treatment of probabilistic soundness as exact. The closing advice on deployment design is removed, because puts evidence design out of scope.
ends with a sample report.

separates whether an evaluation was made from what it found, and notes the related line drawn earlier in . The status that -00 called "not established" is now "not evaluated", because the rules use "establish" for the relation between evidence and a claim. Downgrading is now a reporting practice that applies to both questions, and a claim supported at another base is a separate finding, not a downgrade.

Sections and are shorter. The three public findings move to ; the Grenfell summary now follows the inquiry's wording, and the emissions summary also cites the Notice of Violation . The paragraph on archival preservation moves from to . The discussion of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(e) and the separate paragraph on the considerations-section genre are removed. still names that genre.

corrects the paraphrase of requirement DET-3: -00 omitted the qualifier that limits the cooperation clause to participants whose conduct or assertion is material. The paraphrase now follows the published wording of .
now lists all five distinctions drawn in ; -00 omitted required-target resolution. It also cites sources for the reference-monitor and tamper-evident logging lineages .
narrows its opening sentence, and adds that every finding is conditional on the correctness of the evaluator. The item on unobservable topology now refers to for the reporting terms.
The abstract no longer names the source of the scenario. , , and the Acknowledgments do.

section.name: Acknowledgments
section.t: The scenario of was posed by Stephen Farrell . The mitigation list and the plain statement of the key-custody limit were collected by Shawn Sammartano , who also confirmed the enforcement/observation framing used here ; Charles Eckel proposed that 'a' authorize 'c' to do something specific on 'a's behalf, rather than expose a long-term credential . Dapeng Liu proposed sender-constrained tokens (DPoP) so that 'b' could not present a token bound to 'c's key ; discusses what they do and do not prevent. Yuning Jiang raised the continuity of an identity across restarts, instance changes, and key rotation, which is how the question behind rule 10 of entered this work . The distinction itself is older and is drawn in . Vladimir Ikher is the author's co-author on the earlier work from which the bases of and the ceiling of are restated here. This document also benefited from the broader agentproto and agent2agent mailing-list discussions of 2026 on evidence, delegation, and audit. The author thanks their participants without implying that any of them endorses this document.
Douglas Wadkins reviewed a pre-submission draft; the statement of scope in , the additions to , and the qualification in are responses to his comments.
Blake Morrison contributed the Certificate Transparency omission-control example in .

section.name: Document development disclosure
section.t: This document was drafted with substantial assistance from generative AI tools, working from the author's prior publications, specifications, and mailing-list correspondence, at the author's direction. It also incorporates material arising from adversarial review conducted with such tools: the wording of several rules, and the separation of analytical justification from documented practical confirmation stated in , were reached that way. In -01, the treatment of independence (Sections , , , and ), rules 12 and 13 of , and the reporting terms of were revised or added the same way. In this revision, the Certificate Transparency example in was edited from Blake Morrison's contribution with assistance from such tools. The authorization-status clarification in was also developed with such assistance. The author is responsible for this document's content, citations, and attributions. The use of large language models (LLMs) in IETF discussions is the subject of , which explicitly excludes Internet-Draft and RFC text from its scope. This disclosure is voluntary.

The author also has an implementation interest in this area: the WEXP appraisal layer is the author's own work. This document is usable independently of it. No organizational independence between the two works is claimed.
